The Roosevelt Corollary. In 1904, President Theodore Roosevelt asserted that the United States possessed the right to intervene militarily in Latin American and Caribbean nations to suppress disorder, prevent European intervention, and enforce debt collection. Formulated as an extension of the Monroe Doctrine, Roosevelt justified American intervention as "international police power," positioning the United States as regional hegemon. The corollary represented the apex of American imperialism in the hemisphere and justified repeated US military occupations and interventions in Latin America throughout the twentieth century, profoundly affecting US-Latin American relations.

Roosevelt articulated the corollary in 1904 as a response to instability in the Dominican Republic, arguing that chronic disorder invited European intervention and American intervention was thus necessary. The Monroe Doctrine of 1823 had warned Europeans against colonizing the Western Hemisphere. Roosevelt's corollary reframed it as justification for American dominance rather than European exclusion. Roosevelt justified intervention through the concept of international police power: civilized nations should regulate unstable regions, with the United States assuming this burden in its hemisphere.

The United States intervened in Panama, Nicaragua, Haiti, and the Dominican Republic under the Roosevelt Corollary framework, often establishing protectorates and occupations lasting years or decades. The corollary explicitly linked intervention to debt collection and financial management, positioning US intervention as ensuring hemispheric financial stability and protecting American creditors. Latin American nations condemned the corollary as imperialism, poisoning US-Latin American relations and contributing to persistent anti-American sentiment throughout the twentieth century. The corollary demonstrated how Roosevelt pursued this framework as the cornerstone of his foreign policy, shaping the relationship between the United States and the nations that would bear the consequences of American hemispheric dominance.
